Bristol.region: Bristol and the West of England
Bristol.s1_head: Kitting the visitor economy of the West of England
s1loc: Bristol runs one of the South West's biggest visitor economies, headed by Brunel's SS Great Britain and the Being Brunel museum in the Great Western Dockyard, the Clifton Suspension Bridge over the Avon Gorge and its hillside museum, and the M Shed on the Harbourside. We The Curious on Millennium Square, Bristol Cathedral and St Mary Redcliffe pull steady visitor numbers across the year, with the Bristol Zoo Project at Wild Place drawing families to the city's edge.

The leisure and activity layer is just as busy, from Floating Harbour boat trips and the Bristol Aquarium to the Ashton Court Estate, Brandon Hill and the Cabot Tower above the centre. Wapping Wharf and Gas Ferry Road add waterside leisure, while watersports on the harbour, the SS Great Western Dockyard family attractions and the green space of Castle Park keep activity operators working hard right through the season.

Heritage and culture run deep, from the Georgian terraces of Clifton and the medieval Old City and King Street to the Arnolfini, the Watershed and the Bristol Museum and Art Gallery. The Bristol Hippodrome, the Bristol Old Vic and the Bristol Beacon anchor the stage scene, while Banksy street-art trails through Stokes Croft and the Bristol International Balloon Fiesta at Ashton Court fill the events calendar.

Underpinning it all is a deep city-centre and Harbourside hotel trade and a wide tour-operator and guide scene, with Cabot Circus and the Wapping Wharf quarter drawing day-trip crowds. Bristol Airport at Lulsgate, Bristol Temple Meads station and the M4 and M5 corridor feed visitors into neighbourhoods like Bedminster, Bishopston, Redcliffe and Southville and out to the Mendips and the Severn shore across the season.

Cardiff.s1_head: Kitting the visitor economy of the Welsh capital
s1loc: Cardiff anchors the Welsh visitor economy, headed by Cardiff Castle with its Roman walls and Gothic interiors on Castle Street, the 74,500-seat Principality Stadium hosting rugby internationals and stadium tours, and the National Museum Cardiff in Cathays Park. Cardiff Bay, one of Europe's largest waterfront developments, draws crowds to the Pierhead and the Senedd, while Llandaff Cathedral and the fairytale Castell Coch above the city add to the marquee draws.

The leisure and activity layer runs deep, from Techniquest in the Bay and the Doctor Who Worlds of Wonder experience to Bute Park, Roath Park and its lake, and the Cardiff International White Water centre for rafting and paddling. The Wales National Pool Cardiff, St David's shopping quarter and the Victorian and Edwardian arcades keep family attractions, watersports operators and activity teams busy across the season.

Heritage and culture round it out, with the open-air National Museum of History at St Fagans rebuilding old Welsh village life, the Cardiff Story museum in the Old Library and the Norwegian Church on the waterfront. The Wales Millennium Centre, the Utilita Arena, the New Theatre and a busy events calendar of concerts and shows fill quarters like Cathays, Pontcanna and Mermaid Quay throughout the year.

Underpinning it all is a strong city-centre and Bay hotel trade and a wide tour-operator and guide scene serving rugby weekends and conferences. Cardiff Airport at Rhoose, Cardiff Central station and the Valleys lines feed visitors into Roath, Canton and Cardiff Bay and out along the Glamorgan coast, with day-trip draws from Penarth pier to the castles of the South Wales valleys across the season.

Nottingham.s1_head: Kitting the visitor economy of Nottinghamshire
s1loc: Nottingham draws visitors with its Robin Hood legend at the heart of the offer, headed by the transformed Nottingham Castle and Ducal Palace on Castle Rock, the City of Caves beneath the streets and Wollaton Hall and Deer Park, the Elizabethan mansion used as Wayne Manor in The Dark Knight Rises. The National Justice Museum in the old Shire Hall and Nottingham Cathedral round out the marquee draws across the city centre.

The leisure and activity layer is busy too, from the National Water Sports Centre at Holme Pierrepont and the lakes and white-water course there to Wollaton Deer Park and the Forest Recreation Ground that hosts the Goose Fair. Trent Bridge cricket ground and the City Ground, home of Nottingham Forest, run stadium and behind-the-scenes tours, while the Victoria Centre and intu shopping add family attractions through the year.

Heritage and culture complete the picture, with the Lace Market quarter and Nottingham Contemporary gallery, Ye Olde Trip to Jerusalem cut into the rock and Green's Windmill at Sneinton. The Motorpoint Arena, the Theatre Royal and Royal Concert Hall and the Splendour and Goose Fair events calendar keep the cultural scene busy across the historic city centre and its old quarters.

Underpinning it all is a solid city-centre hotel trade and a wide tour-operator and guide scene serving concerts, sport and city breaks. Good rail and tram links via Nottingham Station and the NET network feed visitors into neighbourhoods like the Park Estate, West Bridgford and Sneinton, with day-trip draws out to Sherwood Forest, Newstead Abbey and the Dukeries across the season.

Brighton.s1_head: Kitting the visitor economy of the Sussex coast
s1loc: Brighton runs one of the South Coast's busiest visitor economies, headed by the Royal Pavilion built as a seaside palace for George IV, the Brighton Palace Pier dating from 1899 and the 162-metre Brighton i360 observation tower at the shore end of the West Pier. SEA LIFE Brighton, the world's oldest operating aquarium opened in 1872, sits opposite the pier, while the seafront and the beach pull steady crowds along the front across the year.

The leisure and activity layer is just as lively, from the Volk's Electric Railway and the seafront arches to Brighton Marina with its watersports, boat trips and waterside leisure. Preston Park, the South Downs above the city and the beach decks at the i360 add activity space, while indoor venues and family attractions along Marine Parade keep operators working hard through every season.

Heritage and culture run deep, from The Lanes maze of antique shops and the bohemian North Laine to the Regency squares of Kemptown and Brunswick and the Brighton Museum and Art Gallery in the Pavilion Gardens. The Brighton Dome with its Concert Hall and Corn Exchange, the Theatre Royal Brighton, the Komedia, the Brighton Festival and Brighton Pride fill a packed events calendar.

Underpinning it all is a deep seafront and city hotel trade and a wide tour-operator and guide scene serving conferences, language schools and city breaks. Good rail links via Brighton Station to London and the coast feed visitors into Hove, Kemptown and the Marina, with day-trip draws along the seafront to Worthing and out into the South Downs National Park across the season.

Plymouth.s1_head: Kitting the visitor economy of Britain's Ocean City
s1loc: Plymouth anchors the South Devon visitor economy as Britain's Ocean City, headed by the National Marine Aquarium, the UK's largest, and Plymouth Hoe with its red-and-white Smeaton's Tower lighthouse and sweeping views over Plymouth Sound. The historic Mayflower Steps, the Mayflower Museum, the cobbled Barbican streets and The Box museum near Drake Circus carry the city's maritime story and draw visitors across the year.

The leisure and activity layer is busy too, from Tinside Lido on the Hoe and boat trips out across Plymouth Sound to Mount Edgcumbe across the water and the new National Marine Park. Central Park, the waterfront watersports scene and family attractions around the Barbican keep activity operators and event teams working through the season, with sailing and diving drawing visitors to the Sound.

Heritage and culture complete the picture, with the Royal William Yard arts and dining quarter in the old naval victualling depot, the Elizabethan House on the Barbican, the Royal Citadel above the harbour and Saltram House on the city's edge. The Plymouth Pavilions arena and the Theatre Royal Plymouth anchor the stage and events scene across the waterfront and the old town.

Underpinning it all is a solid waterfront and city hotel trade and a wide tour-operator and guide scene serving cruises, ferries and coastal breaks. Brittany Ferries sailings from Millbay and Plymouth station feed visitors into quarters like the Barbican, the Hoe, Stonehouse and Devonport, with day-trip draws out to Dartmoor, the Tamar Valley and the South Devon coast right across the year.
